case_name: Anani et al v. Uniglobe Travel (Western Canada) Inc.
text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Anani et al v. Uniglobe Travel
(Western Canada) Inc.,

2004 BCSC 824

Date: 20040618

Docket:
S017139

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Andrea Anani and Ziad Anani

Plaintiffs

And

Uniglobe Travel (Western Canada) Inc.

Defendant

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Rice

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for plaintiffs

Appearing on their own behalf

Counsel for defendant

A.
Morrison

Date and Place of Trial/Hearing:

April
26 – 30,

May 3 – 7

May 10, 11, 13, 14, 2004

Vancouver,
B.C.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The plaintiffs, Mr. and Mrs. Anani,
seek damages against the defendant Uniglobe Travel (Western Canada) Inc. for
breach of contract, wrongful termination of their travel agency franchise at
Sechelt, B.C. and fraud.

[
2
]

Uniglobe terminated the franchise on October 29,
2001, still in the second year of a ten year term.  The Ananis allege that as a
result they suffered a loss of opportunity to earn profits of nearly $500,000
over the following years, and they also allege malice and seek aggravated and
punitive damages.

[
3
]

Uniglobe’s immediate reason for terminating was
a letter circulated by the Ananis on September 25, 2001.  It was one of a
succession of strongly worded messages meant to capture attention and expose a
conspiracy to destroy the Ananis’ franchise.

[
4
]

Uniglobe says the Ananis, not Uniglobe, breached
the agreement and Uniglobe seeks judgment for monies owing and damages for lost
royalties.

[
5
]

Attached as an appendix to these reasons are
excerpts from the letter of September 25, 2001 as well as two of the previous
letters, one dated September 7, 2001 and the other June 15, 2001.  The one of
June 15, 2001 was emailed to Mr. William Hsu, president of Uniglobe
Franchise Owners’ Association (“UFOA”).  The other two were sent directly by
fax to all of the other 80 odd Uniglobe agencies in Western Canada.

BACKGROUND OF THE PARTIES

[
6
]

Uniglobe owns and has owned since 1989 the
Western Canada rights to franchise Uniglobe retail travel agencies.  It is affiliated
with other franchisors of these agencies under the control of Uniglobe Travel
(International) Inc. (“UTI”).  UTI has always owned and licenced through these
franchisors its Uniglobe trademarks and the “Uniglobe System” of management of
the agencies.

[
7
]

Mr. Anani is a retired commercial airline
captain.  He once piloted the largest and most sophisticated of aircraft.  He
is also university educated and has patented inventions.  He professes to be
knowledgeable in international law and international aviation law.  His wife,
Andrea Anani, holds a business degree and has some accounting experience.
Their home, since about 1997, has been in Half Moon Bay, British Columbia.

[
8
]

The Ananis’ affairs with Uniglobe began at their
initiative near the beginning of 1999.  He was then age 63 and she was 40.  They
decided to start a small business and Mr. Anani, exploring the internet,
came upon the Uniglobe website.  He had known of Uniglobe from his years with
the airlines and knew that it had a good name so he contacted them.

ESTABLISHMENT OF THE FRANCHISE

[
9
]

The Ananis met with Uniglobe executives on
January 5 and 6, 1999 and decided to purchase a new Uniglobe travel agency to
be set up in Sechelt, B.C.  They signed a franchise agreement.  The price was
$54,000.  Unfortunately, the bank turned down their first loan application, and
the purchase stalled.

[
10
]

Then for a short while they considered other opportunities, but in
February 1999, Uniglobe reappeared with another proposal.  It was practically
the same as before except that the fee would be $15,000 less.  At that price
the purchase was feasible and the Ananis readily accepted and bought their
franchise on February 22, 1999.

[
11
]

Mr. Anani testified that he inquired about very little before
signing, preferring to trust the word of Uniglobe’s representatives.  He said
that he did not read the disclosure statement given to him or the agreement
itself before he signed.  Neither, he says, did he read any of the policy and
operations manuals and other materials given to him until about a year later.

[
12
]

Neither did he seek independent legal, accounting or other business
advice or seek to gather information from other franchisees.  Mrs. Anani
in her testimony was rather vague about this phase.  She indicated that she
mainly relied on her husband to make this decision for both of them.

[
13
]

However, the Ananis do not plead that they were in any way deceived
or that there was any misrepresentation of fact, and there was no evidence
adduced to that effect.  They admitted at trial that they understood clearly
that Uniglobe offered no guarantee of success and that the projected revenue
and expenses in their disclosure statement should not be taken as an estimate
of what their experience would be.

THE ANANIS’ CLAIMS

[
14
]

The Ananis say that Uniglobe committed fraud at the outset by
switching the “Start-up” type of franchise that they agreed to buy to a
“Start-up Conversion” type, and by having the Ananis sign the franchise
agreement before their business name became registered.  Thus the transaction
was void, they say.

[
15
]

The main claim is that Uniglobe conspired to destroy the Ananis’
business by withholding support (specifically for their 1-800 telephone and their
email service) and by undermining them in their struggles with their employees
and former employees, notably one, Erin Mussellam .

[
16
]

The Ananis say that Uniglobe had no right to terminate, but even so,
it did not give the Ananis the required 30 days notice, and that was a breach
also.

THE TRIAL

[
17
]

The plaintiffs represented themselves at trial and both of them
testified.  They also called as witnesses three current employees of Uniglobe,
Michael Oostveen, Michael Raincock, and Barbara Trainer as adverse witnesses,
and they called two former Uniglobe employees, Ed Buckholz and Dan Evans.

[
18
]

The defendant’s former president and chief witness, Laurie Radloff,
did not appear.  In January 2004, she was kicked in the chest by a horse and
died.  The defendant relied mainly on admitted documents, cross-examination of
the plaintiffs’ witnesses and the direct evidence of two other Uniglobe
franchisees, Douglas Revell and Patrick McEwan.  The trial commenced April 26,
2004 and went for 14 days.

FRAUD

[
19
]

In the Uniglobe disclosure statement, a “Start-up” franchise was
intended for new owners with no existing business or experience as
franchisees.  The franchise fee for it was $54,000.  The “Start-up Conversion”
franchise ultimately given to them was meant normally for purchasers who had
experience and annual sales of at least $1 million in the travel business.  For
this type, the initial fee was $39,000.  For the Ananis, Uniglobe decided to
waive the $1 million annual sales requirement and $15,000 of their fees and
grant them a “Start-up Conversion” franchise.

[
20
]

There was no difference in the second product except for the lower
price.  It provided the same benefits, rights and obligations.  The Ananis
confirmed that they understood this.  There was no misunderstanding, and no
advantage taken by Uniglobe.

[
21
]

Mr. Anani, however, argued that the transfer must be improper
and fraudulent since they did not qualify for a “Start-up Conversion”, lacking
the past experience and $1 million annual sales record.  He cited the
Trade
Practice Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 457, and the
Alberta
Franchises
Act
, RSA 2000, c. F-23.

[
22
]

Mr. Anani was mistaken on this point.  The parties were not
precluded from waiving Uniglobe’s policy.  There was no deception, and
therefore, no breach of the
Trade Practice Act
.  The Alberta

Franchises Act
was inapplicable.

[
23
]

As to the significance of signing the franchise agreement before
they had obtained their official name, the Ananis are again mistaken.  The
Ananis executed the franchise agreement intending to be bound by it personally.
They did not attach any condition precedent that the name registration had to
come first.  When their business became “Uniglobe Sunshine Coast Travel”, it (they)
did not become a different legal entity.

[
24
]

I find that there was no fraud committed by Uniglobe; there was an
effective sale of the franchise to the Ananis.

WITHHOLDING SUPPORT

[
25
]

The franchise was not a joint venture.  It was essentially a licence
of rights, and sale of information and consulting services.  The agreement
“allowed” the franchisee to operate a Uniglobe agency (¶ 2.3).

Franchisee’s Duties

[
26
]

Management of the agency was to be the responsibility of the Ananis
and the agreement spelled this out as follows:

(a)

they would carry the risk of failure; there
would be no guarantee (¶ 1.4);

(b)

they would have no exclusive, reserved or
protected territorial rights (¶ 2.4);

(c)

they would perform faithfully and honestly and
continuously exert their best efforts to promote and enhance their agency (¶
2.5);

(d)

they would select a location and build an office
subject to Uniglobe’s approval (¶ 3.1);

(e)

they would recognize that “an investment in a
Uniglobe agency involves business risks, and that the success of this business
venture is primarily dependent on your business abilities and efforts”
(¶ 3.1(c));

(f)

they would equip and staff the agency, complete
pre-opening training, enroll in the “International Management Academy”, submit
to the International Air Traffic Authority (“IATA”) and offer 24 hour / 365
days per year reservation and travel service (¶ 3.2, 3.3);

(g)

they and Uniglobe would be independent
contractors and owe no fiduciary duty to each other (¶ 7.1);

(h)

they would develop and maintain high and uniform
operating standards based on the concepts of consistency, reliability, and
professionalism and establish and maintain a reputation for a high quality
travel agency exemplifying high client serving standards, ethical business
practices and integrity (¶ 10.1); and

(i)

they would observe high standards of honesty,
integrity, fair dealings and ethical business conduct in all dealings with
customers, suppliers, vendors, Uniglobe and others, including complying with
Uniglobe’s code of ethics (¶ 10.2(q)).

[
27
]

The Uniglobe code of ethics required the Ananis to:

(a)

observe a high standard of professional conduct
in all details of relationships with competitors, associates, clients and the
public;

(b)

maintain an attitude of cooperation in dealings
with Uniglobe and other franchises;

(c)

strive to protect and enhance the Uniglobe name
and image and maintain consistently high standards of professionalism and
performance; and

(d)

conduct business with fairness and integrity and
not engage in any activity or practice which may result in public criticism of
Uniglobe or the travel industry in general.

The Franchisor’s Duties

[
28
]

Uniglobe’s duty was to furnish guidelines and assistance regarding
the Uniglobe System and Standards, which in Uniglobe’s discretion could be in
the form of manuals, bulletins, written reports and recommendations as well as
telephone and personal consultations, meetings and conferences (¶ 5.1 - 5.2).  Impliedly
also, the agreement obligated Uniglobe to give some advice and to provide or
arrange for training, but not to act as a technical service provider.

[
29
]

Otherwise, the agency was independent.  The agreement imposed no positive
obligation on Uniglobe for technical support in relation to software or the
reservation and travel service.  It was the agency’s responsibility to obtain
these for itself and to maintain them.  In particular, it was for the agency to
arrange for its 1-800 number service and internet / email.  Other companies
associated with UTI were equipped to provide some of these services, and the
Ananis could deal with them.

UNIGLOBE’S PERFORMANCE GENERALLY

[
30
]

Uniglobe guided the Ananis through the process of orientation and
training, provided full sets of manuals, methodically taught them the Uniglobe
System, and monitored their progress.  Specific staff was assigned to monitor
and liaise with them.  The records introduced at trial show devoted support
including continual contact with the Ananis and regular agency reviews.  It was
complete and valuable support and with certain exceptions, the Ananis
acknowledged this in their testimony.  Those exceptions are next.

1-800 and Email Problems

[
31
]

Uniglobe would arrange for each franchisor to receive generally all
1-800 calls within 50 kilometres of the franchisor’s area.  In the Ananis’
case, however, a number of those calls began to be diverted to another Uniglobe
agency in North Vancouver.  Also, at certain times, some of their email became
blocked.  Mr. Anani testified that this was because of the email being
“open relayed” by or on the orders of Uniglobe.  In about August 2001, Mr. Anani
also discovered a computer virus emailed to them which could have destroyed
their system.  These were coincidences that in his mind pointed to Uniglobe as
the responsible party.

[
32
]

David Raincock, regional vice president of Uniglobe in charge of new
technology at the time, testified that he investigated when Mrs. Anani
complained about the 1-800 calls.  He solved the problem by seeing that the
company in control of the 1-800 number assigned to the Ananis all of the
telephone prefix numbers for their area.

[
33
]

There is evidence from one memo that the Ananis had applied for
several telephone prefixes before the problem of diversion of their calls
occurred.  It was not clear why that information was not passed on and it may
be that Uniglobe forgot to pass on this information, but that is uncertain.

[
34
]

Mr. Raincock also identified the calls that had been diverted.  He
calculated that the commission loss to the Ananis for those calls not received
was minimal (less than $600).  There was no other evidence of the actual loss
tendered nor any evidence of any significant reoccurrence of the problem.

[
35
]

Mr. Raincock says that as soon as he was told of it, he
investigated the email problem and a memo explaining the problem was sent to
the Ananis on April 1, 2001.  Apparently, the Ananis’ internet service provider
would block email traffic once a certain number of messages passed through
within a certain period.  This was to create a spam filter of sorts.  To solve
the problem, the Ananis had to consult with their service provider, which is
what Uniglobe advised the Ananis to do.  There was nothing more that Uniglobe
could do.

[
36
]

Regarding the virus problem, Mr. Raincock testified that Mr. Anani
could have received it from virtually anyone.  It was a well known worldwide virus.
Like everyone else, the Ananis had to maintain vigilance, and Mr. Anani
had done so.  He had spotted the virus and deleted it, and no damage was done.  Mr. Raincock
denied emphatically that he or anyone else to his knowledge had sent it to the
Ananis.

[
37
]

In
Boston Pizza International Inc. v. Filcan Ventures
(International) Inc. et al.
, (23 November 2001), Vancouver C952134
(B.C.S.C.), Henderson J., in considering a default by the franchisor, stated:

One must view all
of these lapses collectively and assess them against the entirety of the
operation and the entirety of the relationship between the parties.  ...  Overall,
the performance of this franchisor lived up to that which would have been in
the reasonable and objective contemplation of these parties at the time they
entered into the agreement.

[
38
]

I adopt the reasoning of the learned Justice in assessing both
parties’ performance in this case.  So far as the service was concerned,
Uniglobe met its obligations.  I find that it did not by omissions in this
regard breach the agreement.

Office Problems

[
39
]

From the beginning, the Ananis were beset with troubles, and they
fought back.

[
40
]

Before they even got started, there was a bank loans officer whom Mr. Anani
suspected of acting unethically, and he called it to the bank’s attention.  Later,
the Registrar of Travel was suspected by Mr. Anani of conspiring with
someone who did not want the Ananis to have their agency licence.  He warned
the Registrar’s Office that he would inform the public and his lawyer.

Agency Representatives

[
41
]

The Ananis found the agency representatives assigned to them by
Uniglobe rude and vulgar.  The first of them Mr. Anani could tell was
unstable and Mr. Anani became very afraid that the man was forming a
dangerous attraction toward their young employee, Ms. Mussellam , or he
could be.  When Mr. Anani subtly suggested as a cure that the man marry
someone, he took offence.  He was soon replaced.

[
42
]

Ms. Terri Kott was the next representative but Mr. Anani
found her objectionable too.  At their first meeting in mid April 1999, he said
she threatened twice to advise Uniglobe to revoke the Ananis’ franchise.  She
was later replaced.

Trudy McAdam

[
43
]

Observing this conflict, Mr. Anani noted, was Trudy McAdam, who
had been assigned by Uniglobe to help the Ananis manage their office on an
interim basis until their business was up and running.  Thanks to Ms. Kott’s
example of impertinence, the Ananis believe, Ms. McAdam went from a fine worker
to unproductive, argumentative, and dishonest.

[
44
]

In about May 1999, Mrs. Anani caught Ms. McAdam putting
three or four of her friends’ names into a box of names for a customer prize
draw.  The Ananis harshly reprimanded her for that.  On another occasion, Ms. McAdam
allegedly rushed suddenly to Mrs. Anani’s desk and performed something on
the Anani’s computer that, in Mr. Anani’s words, caused it to “commit
suicide”.

[
45
]

Ms. McAdam quit abruptly June 9, 1999 after a confrontation
with Mrs. Anani.  So displeased were the Ananis that they sent Uniglobe an
invoice demanding compensation.  It included items such as:  desertion of work
(when she quit) - $3000; “trauma” from the destruction of the computer -
$1,100; five instances of misconduct - $1000 each; and more.  They sent a
similar invoice for Ms. Kott charging $4,000 for four instances of
misconduct by her.  Uniglobe did not pay.

Erin Mussellam

[
46
]

The first employee of their own was Erin Mussellam , whom Mr. Anani
hired himself.  She started May 1, 1999 and was at first most promising.  But
she too, followed by several others, turned out incompetent, unruly, and
ultimately disloyal.  One after another they were fired or left on angry terms.

[
47
]

The parade of staff coming and going undermined the agency’s success
and particularly in one important way.  It disrupted the continuity of consultant
– customer contact, and the relationship building that went with it.

[
48
]

On or about February 4, 2000, Ms. Mussellam  was dismissed.  By
that time the Ananis had been upset too often by her disrespect and her
manners, e.g. of attending in bare feet, and once by her asking for a salary
raise (they thought about it and decided to refuse; they lowered it instead).  Just
before dismissing her, they thought of another way to change her ways - they
offered her a share in the agency.  She declined.  Mr. Anani says she
remarked, “Why, when I can have it all?”  A signal, he thought.

[
49
]

Within ten days of leaving, she found a new job at Uniglobe
Navigators Travel Ltd. in Kitsilano.  The Ananis protested strongly.  They
believed that she would siphon their clientele and spread false rumours about
them and about the state of their business.

[
50
]

These fears intensified as other employees quit or were fired.  They
became convinced that Ms. Mussellam  was enticing away both their staff
and their clients and that she was spreading it around the Sechelt area that
they were Jewish when they were not.  She reported her departure to IATA
knowing the Ananis had not yet gotten a new manager, which was a condition of
their licence.  On April 4, 2000, Mr. Anani wrote to Ms. Radloff to
summarize a discussion the day before.  In it, he said:

The topics were the improper practices of Erin Mussellam
with regard to I.A.T.A., our office Manager, our Sales Reps., our clients and finally
intruding on the owners personal life.

The most serious
of them all was the issue of personal life intrusion.  Although she knew that
the owners were not from the Jewish faith, she took the liberty to misinform
her audience that they are.  She obviously assumed that the communities on the
Sunshine Coast would be prejudice against the Jews and hence against the
owners...

[
51
]

To the Ananis, Ms. Mussellam  was being rewarded for tarnishing
their reputations and for taking away their business.  They were dismayed that
Uniglobe was taking no step to remove her from the organization.  Mr. Anani
wrote to Uniglobe and demanded her removal.  There followed meetings and
telephone calls but Uniglobe remained unwilling to interfere.

[
52
]

With Ms. Mussellam  still at her job the following spring, the
Ananis turned to “UFOA”.  They wrote but they received no support there.

[
53
]

By September 2001, with nothing changed, they became convinced of a
conspiracy to take away their business.  The proof was evident to the Ananis in
the unnatural coincidence of several events: the rumours, the threats, the
1-800 calls and email sabotage by Uniglobe, the calls to Uniglobe from the
Anani’s employees and former employees, Ms. Mussellam’s alleged takeover
plot, and above all the refusal by Uniglobe to help get rid of her.

THE CONSPIRACY

[
54
]

The Ananis saw Ms. Radloff as the leader of the conspiracy, the
Ananis’ former employees as collaborators, and Ms. Mussellam  as poised to
take over their franchise.  They believed that they had been cut out of
communication with Uniglobe by a “code of silence”.  They were victims of
terror tactics.  They had to fight back.

[
55
]

To be sure, not everyone was a well wisher.  However, there was
important evidence missing.  There was no corroboration of the threats and
sabotage.  No one else knew of the rumours that the Ananis heard which, being
rumours, were hearsay of a quite unreliable sort.  There was no evidence that
the officers of Uniglobe had decided or had expressed a wish to disenfranchise
the Ananis or had discussed the possibility.  The Uniglobe officers who
testified and other witnesses denied knowledge of any conspiracy or campaign or
even common desire, and they said they were certain that no such thing had
occurred.

[
56
]

On the contrary, there were memos to the Ananis from Ms. Trainer,
Ms. Radloff and others encouraging them and offering help in constructive
ways.  Ms. Trainer, Mr. Van Oostveen and the late Ms. Radloff
all attempted in person to reassure the Ananis that there was no conspiracy
against them.  This is documented.  It was to no avail.

[
57
]

Ms. Trainer, who replaced Ms. Kott as the Ananis’ agency
representative, and Mr. Evans, now no longer with Uniglobe, but then a
vice president, both testified that they investigated whether Ms, Mussellam was
enticing away Anani customers.  Mr. Evans said he personally spoke to
Navigators’ owner and told her not to allow any of it, and that he arranged a
meeting face to face between Navigators’ president and Mr. Anani.
Mr. Evans found nothing, and Ms. Trainer was assured when she spoke
to Navigators, that there was nothing to substantiate Ms. Mussellam’s
alleged enticing.

[
58
]

Ms. Trainer said that she and others at Uniglobe did not
believe it was fair to cause Ms. Mussellam’s dismissal.  Even if they had
wished it, they could not.  The Uniglobe franchise agreements forbade hiring of
other franchisee’s employees without consent, but that did not apply to ex-employees.
Ms. Trainer checked and was satisfied that Ms. Mussellam  applied at
Navigators after leaving the Ananis.  Also, nobody could not see a big risk to
the Ananis in Sechelt losing trade to an office in Kitsilano.

[
59
]

In October 2001, the agency was losing money to a serious extent.  Although
due to no fault of Uniglobe, it was no doubt stressful to the Ananis.  The real
reason for most of these troubles was the disruption in their office due to the
Ananis’ manner of dealing with people.

[
60
]

In my opinion, the allegations against Ms. Mussellam and the
allegations of conspiracy and sabotage involving Uniglobe are not supported by
any credible evidence.  In my opinion, Uniglobe provided all of the support and
guidance required of it by the franchise agreement, and probably more.  The
Ananis have not proven that Uniglobe breached the agreement prior to the
termination.  That claim, therefore, is dismissed.

DID THE ANANIS BREACH THE AGREEMENT?

[
61
]

Uniglobe submits that the Ananis, in sending the letters, also
generally by their hostile behaviour, breached their obligations to act
ethically, honestly, professionally, and fairly as required by s. 10.1 and
10.2(q) of the franchise agreement, and by their code of ethics.

[
62
]

Evident from the testimony of Mr. Rebell and Mr. McEwen,
owners of other Uniglobe franchises, was the pride of common good will shared
amongst the franchisees and Uniglobe’s management, including Ms. Radloff.  Mr. Rebell
gave the example of Uniglobe requesting him to help the Ananis during their
first year by handling their ticketing for them, and he did so gladly.

[
63
]

He and Mr. McEwen felt very strongly that the Ananis treatment
of Ms. Mussellam  was unsupportable and wrong, as was their activity
against Uniglobe and Navigators.  It was not fair dealing.  Both spoke in tones
of outrage as if the accusations reflected on them.  Both of them contacted Ms. Radloff
to confirm their support.  Mr. Anani answered that these two were part of
a “club” of larger franchisees.

[
64
]

The letters in question misrepresented facts and were defamatory,
but they were framed as pleas for support to revive democratic rights within
UFOA.  UFOA’s president advised Mr. Anani that his views were not shared.  Mr. Anani
was undaunted.  He attended at the next UFOA meeting on September 11, 2001.  There
his proposals were rejected on a vote of 29 to 0 with 1 abstention.

[
65
]

Interestingly, he left before the meeting started.  He said he
thought it had been cancelled.  It may be that he also sensed the mood of the
meeting.  His reaction when he read the minutes later was to compose his letter
of September 25, 2001.

[
66
]

In that letter, his likening of Ms. Radloff to Bin Laden,
especially so soon after 9-11, and in denouncing her as a liar and a dictator,
all with no factual foundation, was reckless and hurtful and gratuitously so.  It
struck decidedly less as a true call for democracy than as a purposeful
character attack.

[
67
]

The words falsely created an impression of disunity and oppression
within the Uniglobe family with the risk of more to come.  Circulated widely,
the chances of harmful repetition and of reaching suppliers and the public
seemed more than a possibility.  In fact Mr. Anani threatened it expressly
in his letter of June 2001.  He seemed to have the temperament for it, a siege
outlook and a resolve to battle every foe.  His exhibited correspondence is
replete with examples.

[
68
]

On October 22, 1999, Mr. Anani delivered to Uniglobe a self
progress report with this perspective:

They learned a lot from the six months
experience, and therefore, they will not any more tolerate intimidation, threats,
ill manners or disrespect from any body for any reason.  They did give the
benefit of the doubt to the ill mannered.  Not once but many times.  They will
not turn the “other cheek” any more.

The drive behind
the owner’s consistence and persistence is their love for people and the belief
in the excellence of the service of UNIGLOBE to their clients (the
passengers).  This belief will not be shaken by the misbehaviour of a few.

[
69
]

Uniglobe did not for a while challenge the Ananis for their aggressive
behaviour and the periodic inspection reports tended to present them as
progressing very well.  This was the practice particularly of Ms. Trainer -
to accentuate the positive and avoid confrontation with the Ananis.  It did not
excuse the Ananis, however.  There was no waiver of standards in my opinion.  The
messages being sent out by Mr. Anani had become a serious problem.
Evidence shows that Uniglobe advised the Ananis to stop these mass emails.

[
70
]

In my opinion the Ananis, by these communications, failed to conduct
themselves with the good faith, fair dealings and professionalism required by
the agreement, and thus they breached the agreement.

[
71
]

I have concluded that Uniglobe acted on the whole reasonably and in
good faith.  There was no policy or business interest that Uniglobe had or
acted upon to terminate the Ananis’ franchise.  Ms. Radloff and her fellow
officers were driven to do so by the conduct of the Ananis.

CREDIBILITY

[
72
]

Mr. Anani argued that the Uniglobe employees were evasive and
untruthful in giving their testimony.  I do not agree.  There were certain
mistakes exposed due to faulty memory or understanding, but very few and I
found virtually all of their evidence believable.

[
73
]

I was more concerned about the credibility of Mr. and Mrs. Anani.
They were evasive in parts of their testimony.  Much of it was given by way of
presentation of documents, which they would then misinterpret.  Mostly, they
relied on assumptions and suspicions unsupported by any facts.  There was much
speculation of things that were improbable.  I have mentioned examples.

TERMINATION

Termination on Notice of 30 Days

[
74
]

The agreement, clause 15.2(a) allows Uniglobe to terminate:

...30 days after notice of termination to you
on the occurrence of any of the following events and your failure to cure
within such time period:

(iii)   You
fail to comply with this Agreement or any other agreement between you and us;
or

(v)     You
engage in any dishonest or unethical conduct that may adversely affect the
reputation of your UNIGLOBE® Agency or any other UNIGLOBE® Agencies, or the
goodwill associated with the Marks, or

(viii)  You fail to
comply with any one or more of the UNIGLOBE® System Standards or the Servicing
Standards.

[
75
]

In my opinion, Uniglobe had grounds to terminate under all of these
provisions.

Termination for Unauthorised Trademark Use

[
76
]

Clause 15.2(b)(ix) permits Uniglobe to immediately terminate the
franchise if the Ananis make any unauthorized use of the Uniglobe trademarks.  Clause
6.1 requires the Ananis to use the trademarks in compliance with all Uniglobe’s
standards and procedures.  Clause 6.3 states that the Ananis must not use the
Uniglobe trademarks:

...in connection with
the performance or sale of any unauthorized services or products,
or in any
other manner we have not expressly authorized in writing
...  [Emphasis
mine]

[
77
]

Uniglobe argues that clause 15.2(b)(ix) ought to govern instead of
clause 15.2(a) because the breach is incurable and could create a very urgent
threat to the good will associated with the trademark.

[
78
]

I question whether “unauthorized use” was intended to encompass more
than the usual areas such as copying and using the trademark for goods and
services unassociated with Uniglobe.  The ‘use’ made here was for Uniglobe
business.

[
79
]

The power to terminate on immediate notice is formidable and the
intention to confer it should be clear and leave no other reasonable
interpretation.  The parties determined for themselves expressly that a 30 day notice
period would be appropriate for dishonest or unethical conduct that may affect
the Marks.

[
80
]

If Uniglobe’s concern is for unpredictable acts by the Ananis, they
should be reminded that injunctive protection could be sought in an urgent
situation.

Bad Faith

[
81
]

Uniglobe argues that beyond the express obligations in their
agreement, the parties owed a general duty of good faith, which if breached,
would amount to a fundamental breach justifying immediate termination in any event.

[
82
]

In
Shelanu Inc. v. Print Three Franchising Corp
.,
[2000] O.T.C. 768

(Ont. S.C.J.), and
Gateway Realty Ltd. v. Arton Holdings Ltd.

(1991), 106 N.S.R.
(2d) 180
(S.C.) aff’d (1992),
1992 NSCA 70 (CanLII)
, 112 N.S.R. (2d) 180 (S.C.), it was
held that a franchisor / franchisee relationship is akin to a partnership.  It
imposes a duty of good faith, and bad faith is a ground for termination: “‘bad
faith’ [includes] - a conduct that is contrary to community standards of
honesty, reasonableness or fairness.”

[
83
]

In the
Shelanu
case, immediate termination was the
result, but the court did not hold that a finding of bad faith must necessarily
give rise to a fundamental breach.  Fundamental or not, again, I hesitate to
disregard a 30 day notice clause specific to the sort of conduct in question.

[
84
]

I am satisfied that the breach by the Ananis was serious and
undermined the good will between the parties.  Whether it went all the way to
the root of the contract, depriving the defendant of substantially that for which
it had bargained, however, I am not convinced.  In my opinion the evidence does
not quite support fundamental breach as of the date of the termination.

[
85
]

In my opinion, Uniglobe had the right to terminate only on 30 days
notice.

MANNER OF NOTICE

[
86
]

The franchise agreement does not require written notice of
termination, and only where written notice is given, is there required any
particular form of notice.  No particular form of notice is required when given
orally.  Uniglobe witnesses testified to various warnings given to the Ananis
in regard to the correspondence before September 25, 2001.  Examples include: where
Uniglobe told Mr. Anani that what he was doing was “not cool”, or that he
should direct his complaints to them and not others, or when he was told not to
write another letter like the one of September 7, 2001.  Uniglobe submits that it
is those various oral warnings to the Ananis that were sufficient.

[
87
]

None of these qualifies as a proper notice.  A proper notice must
say plainly that termination is intended and when.  Since the only written
termination notice in evidence contained no 30 day warning.

[
88
]

There being no other proof of 30 days notice, I must find that
Uniglobe breached the agreement by failing to give proper notice of termination.

DAMAGES

[
89
]

The Ananis claim compensation for losses up to the date of
termination and for future loss of profits extending to the end of the term of
the franchise agreement in 2008.

[
90
]

They are not entitled to damages for losses up to the date of
termination because Uniglobe was not in breach of the agreement until the
termination date.

[
91
]

The claim remaining is essentially one of loss of opportunity.  It
was for the Ananis to establish on the evidence a real probability of realizing
profits but for the breach of contract.  They must prove that an opportunity
was lost.

[
92
]

Uniglobe will not be relieved from liability merely because the
calculation of damages is difficult.  However, the Ananis must tender all
available evidence to support the claim and there must be enough to establish a
foundation upon which a court may at least make an intelligent guess as to the
value of the loss of opportunity.  The following passage from the Court of
Appeals of South Carolina in
S.C. Fed. Savings Bank v. Thorton-Crosby
,

399 S.E. 2d 8
(1990) at p. 11 as cited in
Murano et al v. Bank of
Montreal et al
(1995),
1995 CanLII 7410 (ON CTGD)
, 20 B.L.R. (2d) 61 (Ont. Ct. Gen. Div.), varied
(1990)
1998 CanLII 5633 (ON CA)
, 41 O.R. (3d) 222 (C.A.) is instructive:

If the fact of
damage is established, the law does not require the amount of damage to be proved
with absolute mathematical certainty; damages may be recovered if there is
evidence upon which a reasonable assessment of the loss can be made. [Cite
omitted]  The estimation of damages, however, cannot be based on conjecture or
speculation; it must pass the realm of opinion not founded on facts and must
rest on evidence from which a reasonably accurate conclusion regarding the
amount of loss can be logically and rationally drawn. [Cite omitted]
There must be a certain standard or fixed method by which the loss may be
estimated with a fair degree of accuracy.

Further,
it was held at ¶ 161:

In assessing the
reliability of projected future profits, a record of past earnings will
obviously increase the certainty of such a prediction. However, a lack of evidence
of past earnings does not automatically preclude a new business from recovering
for lost profits. Rather, a new business must be allowed to prove lost profits
to a reasonable level of certainty by expert testimony, by evidence of actual
profits of similar businesses, by evidence of proven managerial experience and
expertise, and by evidence of subsequent earnings if such evidence is
available. Nevertheless, damages should not be awarded for lost profits which
are entirely speculative and uncertain.

[
93
]

The Ananis argue that they would have earned a net of $13,296 in
November and December of 2001, $78,917 in 2002, $94,201 in 2003 and $65,000 per
year for the following five years.

[
94
]

The figures are taken from projections and benchmarks in Uniglobe’s
disclosure statement.  The projections were derived from a general average of
some other agencies’ results at some time.  The Ananis were cautioned from the
beginning not to rely on them as any indication of what their experience would
be.

[
95
]

The bench mark figures that were used for the last five years of the
franchise term bear no connection to any real experience.  They were simply
taken from an assumption (bench mark) of total annual sales of $3 million.  $3 million
was several times more than the Ananis’ agency ever earned.

[
96
]

These figures are not supported by expert evaluation.  They have not
been considered for adjustment based on the Ananis’ actual past record, or
present dollar value or contingencies.  They are only speculative.  Some kind
of opinion by an expert evaluator was needed in my view.  This was mentioned to
the Ananis, but no expert report was submitted.

[
97
]

Their business sustained losses of $73,220 in 1999, $70,000 in 2000,
and $46,006 in 2001.  They carried on after Uniglobe with another association,
Travel Savers, and the losses thereafter weren’t as high as before, but losses
continued until the agency closed down in January 2004.

[
98
]

How long would it have likely have been before the Ananis would again
breach the agreement and receive a new and valid notice of termination?  At
trial, Mr. Anani was asked if he could have cured their breach within 30
days.  He answered yes “because” it would mean that Uniglobe would finally
listen to his grievances.  Not a promising sign.

[
99
]

It was Mr. Anani who needed to listen but would not.  Instead
he demonstrated that he believed as strongly as ever in the conspiracy.  His
tendency to overact was evident in his testimony at trial and in pre-trial
hearings.  On one interim application at least, he accused counsel for Uniglobe
of unethical conduct.  The charge was baseless and was rejected by the Court
with special costs awarded against him.

[
100
]

What is there to show that any profit at all was
a reasonable expectation?  Evidence including the testimony of Ms. Trainer
portrayed Mr. Anani as easily distracted from important details.  There would
be the Ananis’ tendency to encounter friction with others, including important
contacts.  There would probably continue to be a lack of vital continuity in
keeping consultants, the ones who do most to build the relationships with
customers.

[
101
]

The other franchisee witnesses, Mr. Revell
and Mr. McEwen testified to having very profitable franchises.  No
comparison beyond that was presented and so there was little there to stimulate
hope for the Ananis.

[
102
]

There were other contingencies: the lengthy
aftermath of the New York terrorist attack, the SARS scare, the airline
cutbacks, all of them working downward on passenger travel.  The fact that no
new Uniglobe office has since been established on the Sunshine Coast is
indicative of the value of the opportunity.  It has to be doubted that the
Ananis were going to survive long in this business.

[
103
]

Maintaining the relationships necessary to
succeed in the travel business and working in its competitive environment was
surely a challenge, as perhaps was the Ananis’ chosen location and difficulty
in finding experienced and compatible staff.  Probably other opportunities
would have better suited the style and determination of these plaintiffs.

[
104
]

Even if some profits were possible, certainly it
is still highly improbable that they would have come within the first six
months or one year after the termination on October 29, 2001. Their financial
position was too precarious.

[
105
]

The fact that the agency closed when it did is
an indication that the Ananis were not able to sustain losses for as long as
the term of the agreement.

[
106
]

Combining the probabilities, the near certainty
of an early termination for breach by the Ananis, and the likelihood of no
early profits, the most probable expectation is that there would be no profits
before the agreement ended and thus no losses for which Uniglobe would be
responsible.

[
107
]

In conclusion, I find that the plaintiffs have
not proved that there is any value to the loss of opportunity occasioned by the
defendant’s breach.

[
108
]

In this finding, I have not overlooked the
alternative method of valuing the loss according to the current value of the
plaintiffs’ business as a going concern.  That method was not advanced in
argument or in the pleadings, and again there was no expert opinion.  There was
no basis for valuing positive goodwill and I believe that there was no value to
any business assets on a liquidated basis.  Therefore the result is the same.

UNIGLOBE’S COUNTER CLAIM

Ms. McAdam’s Salary

[
109
]

There was one instance when Mrs. Anani
changed her evidence.  One day she testified that in return for Trudy McAdam’s
assignment to their agency they agreed to pay to Uniglobe two-thirds of her
salary.  The next day she recalled a telephone discussion where Ms. Radloff
agreed to them paying only one-half.  What prompted her, she said, was one
provision she noticed in the counterclaim which specified that the costs would
be shared equally.  Uniglobe’s counsel, confessing embarrassment, advised that
it was a drafting mistake and requested an amendment.  He showed where the
counter claim also indicated two-thirds, and he showed invoices and Mrs. Anani’s
discovery answers where she’d confirmed it was two thirds. I granted the amendment.

[
110
]

I find that the agreement was for the Ananis to
pay two-thirds.  I am satisfied that the earlier evidence, including her own,
is more reliable than Mrs. Anani’s most recent memory revival.

[
111
]

In my opinion, only the course time should be
deducted because it was arranged separately by Uniglobe, but otherwise no more
was discussed than two-thirds \ one-third of her salary.

[
112
]

The obligation of the Ananis extends only to the
last day of Ms. McAdam’s actual employment, which was June 9, 2000.  The
balance payable on that account is $2,695.94.

Claim for Lost Royalties after Termination

[
113
]

Uniglobe says that it was compelled to terminate
the franchise agreement due to the Ananis’ breaches.  That is not in legal terms
precisely correct.  Uniglobe had the right and elected to terminate the agreement
but did so with insufficient notice and thereby placed itself in breach of the
agreement.  It is not entitled to royalties in those circumstances.  Whether
the right would revive at some point was not argued with any factual support.

[
114
]

Neither of the parties addressed the factor of
Uniglobe deciding not to replace the franchise or the question of whether
customers in Sechelt, some of them at least, transferred to other offices at
certain times.

[
115
]

With these uncertainties, I find that there is
no basis for any award for lost royalties.

MEDIATION / ARBITRATION

[
116
]

The Ananis allege breach of the contract by
Uniglobe for not following the mediation / arbitration process in the
agreement.  In fact, they conceded that the first two phases of the process had
taken place, a face to face meeting, and a mutual determination that mediation
would not be followed.  They then elected to litigate rather than arbitrate.

[
117
]

It was equally open for the Ananis to initiate
the arbitration process before they commenced action.  Also, at trial, they
sought no specific remedy for the failure to arbitrate.  In my opinion, the
Ananis attorned to the jurisdiction and waived arbitration, so their claim of
breach on those grounds is dismissed.

COSTS

[
118
]

The parties have requested the permission to
speak to costs in due course.  If no application is made within two weeks of
entry of the order, the defendant will have its costs at Scale 3.

“E. Rice, J.”

The Honourable Mr. Justice E. Rice
